items.title: Ledger's signing kit reports every signature back to Ledger by default
items.idea: An Ambire developer says Ledger's developer kit pings a Ledger server on every signature with network, destination address, device/firmware, app versions and whether the user blind-signed. The reporter was switched on for ETH and SOL on Oct 8. Ledger Donjon says it's how Clear Signing works: the metadata files are too big for the device, so lookups go to Ledger's servers, and nothing is stored.
items.angle: A hardware wallet's whole pitch is that it doesn't trust a server. If 'readable transactions' need a server lookup, the security model has quietly shifted from self-custody toward a hybrid. Watch whether wallet makers fork the kit or ship local metadata.
items.tweetA: You buy a hardware wallet so no server sees your transactions. Then Clear Signing sends the destination address, device and firmware to the vendor on every signature. 'We don't store it' is a policy. It isn't a property of the device.
items.tweetB: Something nobody prices: blind-signing flags are now telemetry. A server that knows which users approve transactions they can't read has a list of the best phishing targets in crypto. That is a honeypot even if nobody abuses it.

items.title: CFTC reportedly warns Kalshi of imminent charges, two weeks after a $40B round
items.idea: Politico and Reuters report the CFTC privately warned Kalshi that enforcement charges could come soon, over whether it properly notified the regulator about dozens of new products listed through self-certification (list next day, no express approval). Kalshi calls it 'a procedural error involving a handful of contracts, many of which weren't live.' This comes from a CFTC under Selig that has backed prediction markets against the states. Kalshi closed $1B at a $40B valuation late October.
items.angle: The federal backstop is the entire legal argument for prediction markets against the states. If the friendly regulator starts enforcing, the 'federal preemption' moat looks thinner. Read alongside Bits + Bips' piece on state bans ($HOOD, $COIN exposure).
items.tweetA: Kalshi's whole defense against 50 state gaming regulators is 'we're federally regulated by the CFTC.' Now the CFTC is warning it about charges. A $40B valuation built on one friendly regulator is also a concentration risk.
items.tweetB: Self-certification means list today, ask nobody. It's the reason prediction markets can put a contract on anything within 24 hours. If enforcement tightens it, product velocity falls, and product velocity is what drove $98B of October volume.

items.title: BTC volume jumped 13x in the 5 minutes after a hot CPI print
items.idea: October CPI +0.4% (core +0.3%), both a tenth above forecast; shelter drove over 0.3pp of the gain, energy +0.7%, used cars -1.2%. BTC fell ~1.2% within minutes to $73,400. 483 BTC traded in the 5 minutes after 8:30 ET vs ~36 BTC in the 5 minutes before. The report had no 12-month rate because October 2025 prices were never surveyed during the 2025 funding lapse.
items.angle: BTC now trades like a rates instrument on macro prints. The bigger macro oddity: no YoY CPI exists for October, so the market is flying with a hole in its main inflation series while Fed speakers talk about hikes.
items.tweetA: 483 BTC in five minutes after CPI vs 36 before. That's 13x. Bitcoin isn't trading as a hedge against the Fed anymore. It's trading as a leveraged bet on the Fed.
items.tweetB: Underrated detail: there is no 12-month CPI number for October. The 2025 shutdown means October 2025 prices were never collected. The Fed is debating hikes on an inflation series with a hole in it.

items.title: MegaETH becomes MEGA: $30M pivot into on-chain AI inference marketplace
items.idea: The MegaETH Foundation is now MEGA and is committing $30M to products on MegaETH, starting with a public AI inference marketplace opening on-chain in December. 'No equity and one token: $MEGA', with the board handling tokenomics, programmatic buybacks and product investment. Network decentralization targeted by end of Q1 2027.
items.angle: L2s pivoting to AI inference is the 2026 version of 2021's 'every chain is a gaming chain.' The real tell is the structure: a token-only entity with buybacks is basically an equity substitute without the shareholder rights.
items.tweetA: MEGA: 'no equity and one token,' with programmatic buybacks run by a board. That's a company with token holders standing in for shareholders and none of their legal rights. The AI pivot is the headline. The structure is the real story.
items.tweetB: Count the L2s that have pivoted to 'AI' this year. When a chain built for speed decides its best product is an inference marketplace, that's an admission that blockspace demand alone didn't pay the bills.

items.title: Binance cuts off MEXC four weeks before the FinCEN ban; $16.7B in alleged illicit flows
items.idea: Binance will refuse transfers to MEXC and affiliates and hold incoming MEXC funds for compliance review, ahead of a FinCEN order barring US institutions from dealing with MEXC from Dec 10. FinCEN says MEXC moved $16.7B in illicit flows May 2021-May 2026.
items.angle: A FinCEN 311-style action now spreads to offshore exchanges before it even takes effect. Binance is acting as an enforcement arm of US AML policy. Liquidity fragmentation risk for MEXC-listed small caps.
items.tweetA: Binance, the exchange that paid $4.3B to settle with the DOJ, is now enforcing FinCEN orders against a competitor before they take effect. US AML policy has an offshore enforcement arm, and it's the former defendant.
items.tweetB: MEXC is where a lot of long-tail tokens list first. If major venues wall it off before Dec 10, those tokens lose their main on-ramp. Watch spreads on MEXC-exclusive listings.

items.title: Ethereum Glamsterdam upgrade stalls: 4 reports of live contracts that could break
items.idea: The Ethereum Foundation received four reports of live contracts that could break under Glamsterdam's proposed gas changes, and asked core devs not to decide until ChainSecurity and Dedaub audits (due ~Nov 16) are public.
items.angle: Ethereum's roadmap is now constrained by backward compatibility with billions in deployed code. That is the cost of being the incumbent settlement layer, and an opening for faster-shipping chains.
items.tweetA: Four live contracts may break, so Ethereum's next upgrade waits on audits. That's what being a settlement layer means: you can't move fast once billions depend on gas costs you set years ago.
items.tweetB: Gas repricing used to be a technical tweak. Now it's a counterparty-risk event for deployed contracts. Mid-November audits are the next catalyst for $ETH roadmap sentiment.

items.title: McHenry: incoming Democratic House can't pass an anti-crypto bill; GENIUS repeal unlikely
items.idea: Former House Financial Services chair Patrick McHenry says the new Congress is more pro-crypto in both parties than those of 6-8 years ago, doubts an anti-crypto bill can pass, and calls a GENIUS Act repeal unlikely. Separately, Bitwise's Matt Hougan says crypto bottomed in June and expects 'a few weeks of uncertainty' and then a good year-end.
items.angle: The midterm 'crypto is doomed under Dems' trade looks overdone if stablecoin law is entrenched. The bigger risk is CFTC/SEC leadership via oversight, not legislation.
items.tweetA: The market priced the Blue Wave as anti-crypto. The man who wrote much of the US crypto law says the new Congress is more pro-crypto in both parties than in 2018. Stablecoin law doesn't get repealed once banks are building on it.
items.tweetB: Legislation isn't the risk. Oversight hearings, subpoenas and agency leadership are. Democrats don't need to pass a bill to slow crypto. They need committee gavels, and they have them now.

items.title: iOS 'worse_query' flaw lets malicious apps read other apps' files; Binance tells users to delete sideloaded apps
items.idea: Binance warned iPhone users to delete sideloaded apps and update iOS. The 'worse_query' flaw lets malicious apps read other apps' local files, which could expose seed phrases and keys. Binance: 'an iOS-level issue, not unique to Binance.'
items.angle: Sideloading was forced open by EU regulation, and now there's a sandbox escape that turns it into a key-theft vector. Regulatory openness and security trade off directly here.
items.tweetA: The EU forced iOS open to sideloading. Now an iOS flaw lets sideloaded apps read other apps' files, seed phrases included. Every 'open the walled garden' rule has a security bill, and crypto users pay it first.
items.tweetB: If your seed phrase lives in an app's local storage on a phone, it was never cold storage. 'worse_query' is the reminder hardware-wallet makers needed. That makes the Ledger telemetry fight today awkward timing.

items.title: Visa stablecoin settlement run rate passes $25B, 10x in a year; Monad joins
items.idea: Monad joined Visa's stablecoin settlement program. Visa's stablecoin settlement run rate passed $25B in September, roughly 10x a year earlier. Moody's also piloted pushing test credit ratings to several blockchains at once via Chainlink CCIP.
items.angle: 10x YoY on an incumbent card network's settlement rail is the cleanest adoption metric in stablecoins. Settlement, not payments UX, is where stablecoins are winning.
items.tweetA: Visa's stablecoin settlement: $25B run rate, 10x in a year. That's not a crypto adoption story. It's a card network quietly moving its own treasury plumbing onto chains. $V
items.tweetB: Moody's pushing ratings on-chain and Visa settling $25B in stablecoins in the same week. The institutions aren't 'exploring' anymore. They're moving their back offices.

items.title: Goldman, Citi and other banks commit $270M to 'Project Faro', a joint dollar stablecoin for H1 2027
items.idea: Per Bloomberg, Goldman Sachs, Citigroup and other banks committed $270M to fund the first five years of a joint US-incorporated stablecoin issuer codenamed Project Faro, targeting a dollar token launch in H1 2027.
items.angle: A bank consortium coin is a direct shot at $USDC and Tether's onshore ambitions. $270M over 5 years is small, which suggests a utility play for interbank settlement, not a retail land grab.
items.tweetA: $270M for five years: that's what the biggest banks in America budgeted to compete with a stablecoin market Tether makes billions on. They're not trying to win retail. They're building an interbank rail and keeping the float.
items.tweetB: Under GENIUS, stablecoins became something banks could issue themselves, and the consortium followed. Circle's moat is now distribution, not the license. $CRCL

items.title: Bitmine lost $6.3B on ETH treasury; 5.9M ETH sits $5.4B below cost; Canaan revenue -90%
items.idea: Bitmine lost $6.3B in the fiscal year ended Aug 31, mostly unrealized ETH markdowns; its 5.9M ETH ended the year ~$5.4B below cost, and internal-control material weaknesses persisted for a second year. Canaan Q3 revenue fell 90% YoY to $14.5M as mining hardware sales fell to $4.8M from $118.6M.
items.angle: Digital asset treasury companies are now forced holders sitting on large losses, which is a supply overhang if any of them must deleverage. Canaan's collapse shows miners aren't buying rigs, which says a lot about hashprice economics.
items.tweetA: Bitmine holds 5.9M ETH, $5.4B under cost, with control weaknesses two years running. The treasury-company trade turned into the largest unrealized loss in crypto, and it's sitting on top of $ETH supply.
items.tweetB: Canaan's hardware sales fell from $118.6M to $4.8M in a year. When miners stop buying rigs, they're telling you hashprice doesn't justify capex. Watch the hashrate trend, not price.

items.title: Alta raises $47.5M Series A for a ZK-private institutional banking chain; Airwallex to build on it
items.idea: Alta raised $47.5M led by Index Ventures with GV, Blackbird, Square Peg and Capital 49 ($80M total), building a blockchain that uses zero-knowledge cryptography to keep institutions' balances, transactions and compliance policies private. Airwallex has said it will build on it. Unchained's Uneasy Money also notes a Hyperliquid perp is already pricing Anthropic's ~$1.4T IPO.
items.angle: Privacy is the missing piece for institutional on-chain finance. ZK chains with a named fintech anchor customer are where serious VC money is going, not consumer L1s.
items.tweetA: Index and GV putting $47.5M into a privacy chain for banks tells you what's holding back institutional on-chain finance. Not speed, not cost. Banks can't put their balance sheets on a public ledger.
items.tweetB: Pre-IPO perps on Hyperliquid are already pricing Anthropic at ~$1.4T before it lists. Crypto rails are becoming the gray-market price discovery venue for private tech.

items.title: Corporate BTC buyers are pulling back: Strive's weekly buys fell from 6,000+ BTC to 29
items.idea: BTC is back at its 200-day MA, threatening the recovery that began in August, with ETF demand weakening. Strive's weekly purchases fell from over 6,000 BTC to just 29, and Strategy is now spending more on preferred-share buybacks than on Bitcoin.
items.angle: The two marginal bids of this cycle, ETFs and treasury companies, are both fading at the same technical level. If $MSTR is defending its preferred stack instead of buying BTC, the reflexive loop is running in reverse.
items.tweetA: Strive: from 6,000+ BTC a week to 29. Strategy: spending more buying back its own preferred than buying Bitcoin. When the biggest corporate buyers start defending their capital structure, the treasury bid is gone.
items.tweetB: BTC sitting on its 200-day with ETF flows weak and corporate buyers gone. Who's the marginal buyer now? If nobody can answer that, the 200-day won't hold. $MSTR $IBIT

items.title: The 3 arguments against an AI bubble are steps 1-3 of every bubble
items.idea: Packy lays out a 10-step capital cycle: a miracle technology arrives, early suppliers earn scarcity profits, demand looks bottomless, capital and competitors pile in, everyone builds at once even if they see the glut coming, supply arrives and prices collapse, capital loses and consumers win, then a low-cost consolidator wins. The usual anti-bubble arguments (real utility, real revenue, labs can be profitable) are exactly steps 1-3.
items.angle: This is the cleanest framing for being long AI usage and skeptical of AI capital returns at the same time. The trade is consumers and low-cost integrators, not the capacity builders paying scarcity prices.
items.tweetA: 'AI is useful, the revenue is real, the labs are profitable' isn't an argument against a bubble. It's the description of step one. Railways, oil and fiber all had real demand. The capital still got wiped out.
items.tweetB: The question isn't whether AI is real. It's who captures it. Fiber traffic grew 130% the year Global Crossing left bankruptcy, and revenue still fell 6%. Demand growth and investor returns are different charts.

items.title: Anthropic S-1: $900.9B of compute committed through 2045, half before 2030
items.idea: Anthropic's S-1 shows $900.9B in compute commitments through 2045, about half before the end of the decade. Earlier this year Dario said that buying $1T/yr of compute and only making $800B of revenue would mean 'no hedge on earth' could stop bankruptcy. Anthropic was operating-profitable in Q2 and would have been in Q3 excluding ~$2B of noncash donation-matching charges.
items.angle: The S-1 commitment number is the single best stress-test input for the IPO. ~$450B before 2030 has to be covered by revenue growth, and Dario's own framing says the margin for error is about a year.
items.tweetA: Anthropic committed $900.9B to compute. The CEO's own words: be off by a year and 'you destroy yourselves.' Every buyer of the IPO is taking a timing bet with no hedge, and he told you that on a podcast.
items.tweetB: Do the math: ~$450B of compute before 2030 is ~$90B/yr for five years. That's fine at today's growth rate. It's catastrophic if growth falls to the industry average. The IPO prices the first case.

items.title: The fiber bust in numbers: NY-LA circuit went from $1.8M/yr to under $150K in two years
items.idea: Long-haul US fiber doubled 1996-2001 (100k to 200k miles) while electronics lifted per-strand capacity 40x (2.5 to 100 Gbps), on ~$500B of telco spend. TeleGeography: bandwidth prices fell ~70%/yr for three years; a 155 Mbps NY-LA circuit went from $1.8M/yr (2000) to under $150K (early 2002). Qwest went from $91B to $1.9B. The '100 days doubling' stat traced back to WorldCom's buildout pace, which was supply, not demand.
items.angle: The GPU parallel: Epoch shows GB300 serves ~25x the H100's agentic inference despite 2.5x the FLOPs. That's fiber's 40x-per-strand moment. Rental prices for older capacity are the price to watch (Innes / Simon White).
items.tweetA: Fiber 2000: per-strand capacity up 40x, prices down 70% a year. GPUs 2026: GB300 serves 25x the H100's inference on 2.5x the FLOPs (Epoch). Same physics. Ask who's still paying 2024 prices for H100 leases.
items.tweetB: The 'internet traffic doubles every 100 days' number that justified $500B of fiber came from WorldCom's own buildout pace. Supply quoted as demand. Check the sources on today's 'tokens demand' charts.

items.title: Nordhaus: producers capture only ~2.2% of the social surplus from innovation
items.idea: Yale's William Nordhaus (Schumpeterian Profits in the American Economy) found producers captured ~2.2% of the total social surplus from innovation over 1948-2001, with consumers taking ~97-98% via lower prices, better products and higher real incomes. His read on the dot-com bubble: investors 'overestimated the appropriability of innovations.'
items.angle: The base rate for AI value capture by builders should be low single digits of surplus created. Bulls need a reason AI breaks Nordhaus, like a winner-take-all market. That's the real debate.
items.tweetA: Nordhaus: inventors keep about 2% of the value they create. Consumers get 98%. If AI creates $10T of surplus and follows history, that's $200B for producers, about what the hyperscalers spend on capex in one year.
items.tweetB: Being long AI and long AI equities aren't the same bet. History says the surplus goes to whoever uses the technology. The best AI trade might be the companies with the most labor to automate, not the ones selling compute.

items.title: Oil 1860: $20 a barrel to 10 cents in 18 months; Pithole land went from $2M to $4.37
items.idea: After Drake's 1859 well, oil fell from $20/bbl to $0.50 by June 1861 and $0.10 by December. Prices rebounded above $8 in 1864, drawing an even bigger frenzy. Pithole farmland sold for $2M in 1865 and was sold back to the county for $4.37 in 1878. ~600 petroleum companies sought $500M. Standard Oil alone later outgrew that, worth $1.1B in 1911. Similar stories: ~2,000 US automakers shrank to 3 with 90% share; Level 3, the 'winner' of fiber, sold 97% below peak.
items.angle: Investors usually size the market right and get the competition wrong. In AI, the market isn't asking who the Rockefeller (low-cost vertical integrator) is. Packy's answer: companies that can swap in better models cheaply.
items.tweetA: Oil investors in 1865 were right about the market: one company later was worth more than all 600 of them combined. They were wrong about who'd get it. Sizing the market isn't the hard part. Surviving the glut is.
items.tweetB: Level 3 did everything right in the fiber bust: raised money at the top, built 12 conduits, had Buffett's backing, bought rivals cheap. It still sold 97% below its peak. Picking the winner isn't enough if you overpay for it.

items.title: Anthropic used frontier Claude to weaken NVIDIA's CUDA moat
items.idea: Packy notes Anthropic used frontier Claude models to weaken NVIDIA's CUDA moat, so it and others can more easily move off the dominant GPU supplier. He argues AI speeds up both imitation and the build-up of advantage, so moats matter more than ever. Cornered resources (regulated entry, patents) and process power (ASML) are the exceptions to the capital cycle.
items.angle: If AI can port kernels and tooling cheaply, CUDA lock-in, a big part of $NVDA's margin premium, decays faster than consensus expects. Epoch shows Broadcom TPU shipments doubling in one quarter, which fits.
items.tweetA: The model that NVIDIA's chips trained is now helping port software off NVIDIA's chips. CUDA was a moat made of code, and code is the first thing AI commoditizes. $NVDA $AVGO
items.tweetB: Broadcom shipped twice as much TPU compute this quarter (Epoch). Anthropic is using Claude to make leaving CUDA easier (Not Boring). Two separate data points, same direction.

items.title: CoreWeave beat-and-raise reignites AI: semis +5% pre-market, memory more, Kospi +2.5%
items.idea: CRWV beat on earnings and revenue and raised sales guidance after the close. Semis were up 5%+ pre-market with memory up more; S&P futures ~+1%, Nasdaq ~+2%. The bond market was closed for Veterans Day. Asia rallied (Kospi +2.5%, Japan +1%, China +0.5%) except Hong Kong (-1% on Alibaba, Tencent, Xiaomi). Bespoke: names are 'all still well below their highs.'
items.angle: The AI trade's health check now runs through its most levered neocloud, not $NVDA. A rally on a day bonds can't trade means the rates test is postponed, not passed.
items.tweetA: The AI trade got its relief rally from CoreWeave, the most levered neocloud, on a day the bond market was closed. Ask again tomorrow when Treasuries reopen after a hot CPI. $CRWV $SMH
items.tweetB: Kospi +2.5%, Hong Kong -1% on the same AI headline. Korea is the memory trade. Hong Kong is China platforms. The market is drawing a clear line between who sells picks and who has to buy them.

items.title: Fed speakers are laying groundwork for hikes beyond December
items.idea: With no data due to the holiday, Bespoke notes 'a number of Fed speakers... have laid the groundwork for hikes beyond December.' German October CPI fell 0.2% m/m, in line; Italian industrial production rose 1.2% vs 0.7% expected.
items.angle: A hiking Fed alongside a falling German CPI widens US-EU policy divergence, which supports the dollar and pressures long-duration growth. It's the macro headwind Bulltard and Boockvar flag too.
items.tweetA: Fed speakers are talking about hikes after December. German CPI just printed -0.2% m/m. If US inflation stays sticky while Europe's falls, the policy gap goes into EUR/USD.
items.tweetB: Everyone's watching whether AI capex survives the midterms. The bigger threat to long-duration tech multiples is a Fed hiking into 2027. CoreWeave beat. The discount rate didn't care.

items.title: S&P has gained in 67% of Veterans Day-to-Thanksgiving windows since 1954 (avg +0.36%)
items.idea: Since 1954, the S&P 500 has averaged +0.36% between Veterans Day and Thanksgiving, positive 67% of the time, with performance improving in more recent history.
items.angle: Weak seasonality. Useful as a base rate for late-November positioning, not a signal on its own, especially with rate-hike risk live.
items.tweetA: S&P between Veterans Day and Thanksgiving: up 67% of the time, average +0.36%. A coin flip with a slight tilt, against a Fed talking hikes. Seasonality is the weakest argument for owning this tape.
items.tweetB: Bespoke says the Veterans-to-Thanksgiving window has been better in recent years. That's the period of passive inflows and buybacks. Seasonal edges come from flows, so check the flows before trusting the calendar.

items.title: Goldman sees 2.2% US consumption growth in 2027, but the consumer now runs on equity wealth
items.idea: Goldman's Pierfrancesco Mei (Nov 9, '2027 Consumer Outlook: Steady Through the Shocks') forecasts 2.2% consumption growth in 2027 on recovering real incomes, household wealth and broader purchasing power, and argues the low savings rate hides more resilience than it shows. Innes's caveat: the consumer increasingly depends on equity-market wealth, and the AI selloff tests how durable that is.
items.angle: US consumption is now indirectly long the AI trade through the wealth effect. An AI drawdown is a consumption risk, not just a portfolio risk, which links Nasdaq vol to retail and services names.
items.tweetA: Goldman: 2.2% consumer growth in 2027. The fine print: that consumer is funded by stock-market wealth, and the stock market is funded by AI capex. US spending is a leveraged bet on hyperscaler capex now.
items.tweetB: A low savings rate 'hides resilience' only if asset prices hold. When equities are the savings account, a 20% AI drawdown is also a hit to consumption. $XLY

items.title: Welcome to B2A: agents are now the majority of web traffic; Shopify AI orders up ~13x
items.idea: a16z says agents are now most of web traffic, write over half of new online articles and generate most production code. Shopify: AI-driven store traffic up 8x YoY in Q1'26, AI-search orders up ~13x. Human Security: agentic browser traffic up 8x Aug-Oct, Muse 60% of activity and OpenAI products 30%. An estimated 11% of US shopper journeys already pass through AI before a transactional site. OpenAI just launched Businesses in ChatGPT (1.2B WAU).
items.angle: Distribution is moving from search and app stores to agents. Losers: companies that rely on human attention (ads, SEO, comparison sites). Winners: agent payment, identity and fraud rails, a16z's named bottleneck.
items.tweetA: Retailers spent 20 years building CAPTCHAs to keep bots out. Shopify now says AI-driven orders are up 13x. Next decade's growth hack is letting the bots in.
items.tweetB: If agents pick the product, brand marketing to humans loses value and structured product data gains it. The ad-funded internet's customer is changing from a person to a parser. $GOOGL $META $SHOP

charts.desc: Charts inside: B2A market map of agents and infrastructure. Worth opening

items.title: Coding agents preview the agent economy: 40% of GitHub PRs now start with an agent draft
items.idea: As of Sept 2026, 40%+ of GitHub PRs started from an agent's draft vs 17% six months earlier. Supabase: 60%+ of new databases launched by AI tools (June '26). Neon: agents deploy 80% of new DBs. Stripe: agents are ~40% of docs traffic and 70% of CLI API-resource requests. Vercel: agent-triggered deploys up 28x in 12 months. Fewer than 1% of the global workforce are developers.
items.angle: The developer tool stack is the first sector where the buyer is a machine. Infra that agents pick by default (Supabase, Vercel, Stripe) builds a distribution moat that human devrel can't match.
items.tweetA: Agent-started GitHub PRs: 17% to 40% in six months. Vercel agent deploys: 28x in a year. Developers are 1% of the workforce. That's the adoption curve for the first 1%. Run it on the other 99%.
items.tweetB: When agents launch 80% of new Neon databases, the default in the model's training data is the sales team. Being the tool Claude reaches for first is the new enterprise GTM.

items.title: Agent infrastructure is already straining at low volume: payments, fraud, identity
items.idea: a16z says infrastructure is already showing strain at fairly low agent volume in payments, fraud and identity, and communication (iMessage, calls, email). Most enterprises still block agent traffic over fraud and chargebacks. Platforms are adding identity lending (Sign in with ChatGPT), and Claude lets enterprise admins connect plugins org-wide.
items.angle: Chargebacks are the hidden friction. Whoever underwrites agent-initiated transactions (card networks, Stripe, identity vendors) becomes the toll collector. Ties to Visa's $25B stablecoin run rate.
items.tweetA: Every agent purchase raises a question card networks never had to answer: who authorized this? Whoever answers it gets paid on every agent transaction. That's the B2A toll road. $V $MA
items.tweetB: Enterprises block agents over chargebacks today. That's where e-commerce was in 1998, blocking credit cards over fraud. The fraud layer was the business then too.

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (data center backlash)
items.title: The one price to watch: GPU rental rates, as Democrats threaten the data center buildout
items.idea: After the midterms, several states with big data center footprints posted large electoral swings, raising the odds of construction limits. Bloomberg's Simon White argues GPU rental prices are the real signal: if new builds slow, existing compute gets scarcer and more valuable, which rewards hyperscalers with installed capacity and pressures labs, neoclouds and suppliers. Modo Energy estimates 40% of announced data center projects could be disrupted.
items.angle: A build moratorium is bullish for installed capacity and bearish for capex suppliers. That's the split Mattin flagged ($AMZN -2.19% vs $AMD/$MU -17%). Rising H100 rental prices would confirm it.
items.tweetA: Blocking new data centers doesn't kill AI demand. It reprices the data centers that already exist. If 40% of projects stall (Modo), the best AI stock might be whoever owns the most powered megawatts today.
items.tweetB: Data center politics flips the AI trade. Capex suppliers sell less, landlords of installed compute get paid more. Watch GPU rental rates, not headlines. $AMZN vs $MU

items.source: Stephen Innes / Dark Side of the Boom (data center backlash)
items.title: Hedge funds have already cut a lot of AI risk; retail is still holding
items.idea: Innes notes hedge funds have already cut substantial risk while retail positioning remains relatively resilient. The next test is whether rising compute prices can offset slower capital spending.
items.angle: Institutional de-grossing alongside sticky retail is the setup for violent squeezes both ways. That's what Bulltard describes, with CRWV +20% in a day while still below the 21 EMA.
items.tweetA: Hedge funds de-grossed AI. Retail held on. That's why CoreWeave can rip 20% in a day and still sit below its 21 EMA. Short-covering rallies look strong because the buyers are covering, not adding.
items.tweetB: When the pros are out and retail is in, the next leg depends on whether the pros re-enter. That needs a reason, and GPU rental prices rising would be one.

items.title: Boockvar: the Fed needs a view on AI capex. Gold and real rates in focus after CPI
items.idea: In a MRKT Call video with Guy Adami, Boockvar covered the CPI report and the PPI preview, how the Fed is likely to handle inflation, and how rising rate expectations are shaking up the AI trade. He argued the Fed needs a view on AI capex's macro implications, plus updated views on gold, real rates and the dollar. (Email is a short summary of the video.)
items.angle: AI capex is now big enough to be a macro variable: it adds to demand, power prices and imports. A Fed that ignores it misreads both inflation and growth.
items.tweetA: AI capex is now a monetary policy variable. It's large enough to move power prices, import demand and GDP. If the Fed models it as 'tech sector news,' it's missing one of the biggest demand drivers.
items.tweetB: Hot CPI, a Fed talking hikes, and gold still holding up. If real rates rise and gold doesn't fall, the market is pricing something the Fed isn't saying out loud.

items.title: WTI in the $80s after a waterfall from $100+ since the 'Blue Tsunami'. Is all of it Iran war premium?
items.idea: Haymaker says most oil observers think WTI is in the $80s rather than $60s-$70s only because of the Iran war. Prices were over $100 not long ago and have fallen sharply since last week's 'Blue Tsunami' midterm result. The headline frames a supply-starved oil capex cycle that could become an investment feast.
items.angle: If the war premium is the whole story, a ceasefire takes WTI to the $60s. If years of underinvestment set a higher floor, $80 is fair value. The capex angle argues for the second.
items.tweetA: WTI fell from $100+ to the $80s on an election, not a barrel of new supply. If the midterms can move oil $20, the 'war premium' was partly a political premium.
items.tweetB: Consensus: strip out Iran and oil goes to $60s. Counter: a decade of starved capex means $60s don't bring supply back. The war is the premium. Underinvestment is the floor. $XLE $XOP

items.title: Robinhood's event contracts ($173M) now out-earn crypto ($120M), and states are shutting off sports
items.idea: Robinhood event-contract revenue went from $27M a year ago to $173M in Q3 2026 (~12% of net revenue); crypto trading fell to $120M from $268M. Robinhood halted new sports contracts in Michigan and Ohio (Nevada last year) and sued Missouri on Monday. Coinbase stops in Ohio Nov 13. Coinbase's Kalshi-powered business is at $200M+ annualized (~4% of revenue), over 50% non-sports.
items.angle: $HOOD's fastest-growing line depends on a federal preemption theory that is losing in the appeals courts. With today's Kalshi CFTC warning too, it's a real overhang.
items.tweetA: Robinhood now makes more from betting on games ($173M) than from crypto ($120M). Event contracts grew 6x in a year. That's the line states are shutting down one at a time. $HOOD
items.tweetB: Coinbase says over 50% of its event contracts are non-sports. Robinhood's are mostly sports. If the states win, the mix difference matters a lot. $COIN is less exposed to the ban risk than $HOOD.

items.title: Two of three appeals courts side with the states; Supreme Court could take it up in January
items.idea: The Third Circuit leaned Kalshi (NJ, April); the Ninth went for Nevada (Aug); the Sixth held federal law 'neither expressly nor impliedly preempts' Ohio/Tennessee gambling laws (Sept); the Second Circuit refused to pause NY/CT actions (Nov 3). Michigan ordered Kalshi to block residents, with fines up to $500K/day. Arkansas sued Nov 4. The CFTC's Nov 5 interpretation says exchanges may not block customers by state, effective Tuesday, putting firms between a regulator and court orders.
items.angle: A circuit split on preemption almost guarantees cert. The binary is a January Supreme Court decision, a dated catalyst for $HOOD, $COIN, $DKNG and $FLUT.
items.tweetA: The CFTC says you can't block customers by state. Michigan's court says block Michigan or pay $500K a day. When a federal regulator and a state court give opposite orders, the Supreme Court takes the case.
items.tweetB: The prediction market fight is the best catalyst sportsbooks have had in years. If SCOTUS sides with the states, the state-licensed books keep their moat. $DKNG $FLUT are the other side of the $HOOD trade.

items.title: Kalshi's October volume hit a record $98.2B; Polymarket fights on in Ohio
items.idea: Kalshi's October volume hit a record $98.2B; it was valued at $40B in a $1B round that closed Oct 29. Polymarket's US app started opening to a waitlist in Dec 2025 and faces suits from Wisconsin (April), Kentucky (June) and New York (Sept); it is suing Ohio instead of stopping sports contracts.
items.angle: $98B a month annualizes to over $1T notional. That's sportsbook-industry scale on a federal derivatives license, which explains why states are fighting it.
items.tweetA: Kalshi: $98.2B traded in October. Annualized, that's over $1 trillion, more than the whole US legal sports betting handle, done under a derivatives license. That is why the states are fighting.
items.tweetB: Kalshi: record month, $40B valuation, and a CFTC enforcement warning in the same two weeks. Peak volume and peak legal risk together.

items.title: Gifting is back as cold email dies; 'proof-of-work outbound' wins AI security deals
items.idea: speedrun's Head of GTM Macy Mills says gifting is back in fashion 'as cold email becomes less and less effective.' SR007 founders: Kairo (AI security) offers a free scan of the prospect's own environment instead of a demo ('proof-of-work outbound'). Rollup treats sales calls as co-design sessions (first 10 customers). Primitive Labs starts enterprise GTM on day one, with hyperscaler partnerships and Sony backing for credibility.
items.angle: AI-generated outbound has made cold email nearly worthless. Value moves to costly, hard-to-fake signals: physical gifts, free work, in-person dinners. It's the same 'creature residual' logic Mattin applies to consumers.
items.tweetA: AI killed cold email by making it free. Founders are now sending physical gifts and doing free security scans. When a signal costs nothing to fake, buyers start trusting the expensive ones.
items.tweetB: 'Proof-of-work outbound': instead of a pitch, scan the prospect's stack and show what you found. In a world flooded with AI demos, the only credible demo runs on the customer's own data.

items.title: Nvidia board investigates Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy (Megaspeed)
items.idea: TWiST covers the Nvidia board's probe into Jensen Huang's relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, tied to chip buyer Megaspeed (CNBC, Fortune), plus Shaun Maguire on nation-state kompromat. Calacanis's lesson: anyone influential should assume they're a target, including people one or two steps removed (investors, IT staff with keys to the kingdom).
items.angle: Key-person risk at the world's most valuable company now includes counterintelligence. Any finding that links export-control evasion to the CEO's circle would hit $NVDA's China business and its standing in Washington.
items.tweetA: The most important CEO in AI is the subject of a board probe over a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Export controls have been the US's main AI policy tool. Now the question is who was inside the building. $NVDA
items.tweetB: Megaspeed, a chip buyer, is at the center of the Nvidia story. If chip diversion runs through intermediaries close to leadership, every export-control assumption in the China compute numbers needs rechecking.

items.title: Sequoia unwinds 20 years of expansion; Scouts and Arc programs shut
items.idea: TechCrunch: Sequoia is 'hitting rewind', undoing 20 years of expansion. FT: partners were blindsided by Roelof Botha's SpaceX board seat. Calacanis thinks Scouts and Arc were shut because nobody left at the firm wanted to run them, not to punish Botha, and that a new generation wants faster founder response than the old wait-for-Monday-partnership-meeting rule.
items.angle: When the top VC brand contracts, it says concentration is winning: fewer, larger bets on mega-rounds (Thinking Machines, labs) over seed-scale networks.
items.tweetA: Sequoia is shrinking back to its core, cutting the scout network that found a generation of seed deals. In an era of $5B rounds for AI labs, the elite firms are choosing concentration over coverage.
items.tweetB: 'Experiments need champions': when the person who built a program leaves, the program dies. That's as true of every corporate AI pilot as it was of Sequoia Scouts.

items.title: Thinking Machines nears $5B at $40B; Tesla winds down Cybertruck to make room for Cybercab
items.idea: Links from TWiST: Thinking Machines (Mira Murati) nears a $5B round at a $40B valuation and launched Inkling 2 Small. Nous Research released Arete-27B. Tesla will wind down Cybertruck production to make room for Cybercab. Axios says the Democratic wave has the robotaxi industry sweating; CNN asks what Musk's Texas bet means for his companies. Scientific American: dueling proofs from OpenAI and Anthropic astound scientists.
items.angle: Robotaxi regulatory risk just rose with the midterms, and Tesla is moving line capacity toward Cybercab anyway. That's a big capital-allocation bet into a less friendly policy setting.
items.tweetA: Tesla is killing Cybertruck production to make Cybercabs, the same week Axios reports the Democratic wave has robotaxi companies 'sweating.' Retooling a factory for a product that depends on regulators' approval. $TSLA
items.tweetB: Thinking Machines: $40B, the same valuation Kalshi just got. A model lab and a betting exchange priced the same. The 2026 private market has one price for 'category leader.'

items.title: Post-midterm split: Amazon -2.19% vs AMD and Micron -17%. The market repriced the chip supply chain
items.idea: Mattin lists the recent shocks: anxiety over the weakest AI borrowers (CoreWeave and other neoclouds), then Alphabet's second cash-flow-negative quarter ever (the first was earlier this year), then the midterms. After the midterms, moves split by capex buyer vs seller: Amazon -2.19%, AMD -17%, Micron -17.5%. Raoul Pal is 'not selling, and not adding yet.'
items.angle: The market is pricing a capex cut, not a demand cut, which fits Innes/Simon White's thesis on GPU rental prices. Spenders get rewarded for spending less; suppliers take the hit.
items.tweetA: After the midterms: Amazon -2%, AMD and Micron -17%. The market isn't saying AI demand is dead. It's saying the hyperscalers will spend less, and that the buyer of capex wins while the seller loses. $AMZN $MU $AMD
items.tweetB: Alphabet just posted its second negative free-cash-flow quarter ever, both this year. When the richest company in tech burns cash on capex, the supply chain's revenue depends on how long that lasts. $GOOGL

items.title: The Creature Residual: as AI commoditizes output, value flows to the authentically human
items.idea: Mattin's thesis: AI and robotics will push prices down across knowledge work, content and physical goods, so displaced spending flows to what machines can't make: human presence, craft, heritage and live experience. Two drivers: an income effect (gains accrue to the rich) and a status effect (scarcity confers status). He builds a 9-name basket in four sub-themes (Live Spectacle, Heritage and Story, Embodied Experiences, Human Culture), including a fashion house, a cruise line and a heritage car brand, plus one controversial short.
items.angle: A real AI second-order trade outside semis: long scarcity of human experience, short commoditized creative services. Pairs with Nordhaus. If consumers capture 98% of the surplus, they spend it somewhere.
items.tweetA: Everyone has a view on what AI destroys. Almost no one has one on where the displaced spending goes. Mattin's answer: things a machine can't make: live events, heritage brands, travel. The AI trade most people aren't positioned for.
items.tweetB: Nordhaus says consumers keep 98% of innovation's surplus. If AI makes design, code and content nearly free, that freed-up income goes somewhere. Look at the luxury experience data before arguing it's going to more software.

items.title: Experiences beat goods: travel spending's share at its highest since 1960; luxury bookings +30%
items.idea: McKinsey: travel experiences grew 4% (2023-25) vs non-essential goods 0.8%. Travel's share of consumer spending is at its highest since 1960. WSJ: in 2025 US landlords leased more commercial space to service/experience tenants (gyms, spas, wellness) than to traditional retailers, a first. Bain-Altagamma Spring 2026: luxury goods +1-4%, luxury experiences +3-7%, dining/leisure/entertainment bookings ~+30%. AI losers: Chegg -99% from peak, Duolingo -75%, WPP -70% (lost Mars, PepsiCo).
items.angle: The data has supported the experience economy for 25 years. AI is a possible accelerant. Commercial real estate is already moving: experience tenants now beat retail in new leases.
items.tweetA: For the first time, US landlords leased more space to gyms, spas and experiences than to retailers. Commercial real estate is repricing around what you can't buy online, and now what AI can't make.
items.tweetB: Chegg -99%, Duolingo -75%, WPP -70%. That's the AI-loser basket. The winner basket is the hard part, and luxury dining bookings +30% vs luxury goods +1-4% is a hint where it is. $DUOL $WPP

items.title: An open-weight model (GLM 5.3) autonomously hacked 6 Firefox versions for ~$1,000 each
items.idea: In Epoch's offline sandbox, GLM 5.3 compromised the six most recent Firefox versions (200M+ users) for ~$1,000 each, without human input. It reverse-engineered attacks from security patches that hadn't reached users yet (the 'patch gap'), building webpages that read files from visitors' computers and send them to the attacker. Epoch couldn't replicate it on Chrome, but says better prompting or a stronger model could change that. Patch gaps exist in browsers, phone OSes and router firmware.
items.angle: Exploit cost just collapsed to $1K, using a freely downloadable model. That's structurally bullish for patch automation and endpoint security, and bearish for slow-patching vendors. Pairs with Transformer's Hugging Face story.
items.tweetA: $1,000 for a working Firefox exploit, built by a free open-weight model with no human help. The zero-day market used to price these in six figures. Cybersecurity's cost curve just inverted. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: The 'patch gap' used to be safe because exploiting it needed elite skill. Now a downloadable model reads the patch and writes the attack before you've updated. Release practices built for human attackers no longer work.

items.title: Claude Fable 5.2 sets an Epoch Capabilities Index record of 174, above the reasoning-model trend
items.idea: Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2 (released Nov 9) scored 174 on Epoch's ECI vs the prior high of 169 (GPT-6 Astra), above what the post-2024 reasoning trend predicted. Epoch moved ECI to a Bayesian method: Astra now has a 72% probability of beating Claude Opus 5.5 and 99% of beating Fable 5.1. Epoch notes discussion of AI contributing to AI R&D, but says this is one data point.
items.angle: An above-trend jump right before an IPO strengthens Anthropic's 'self-improving lead' bull case (Not Boring). Watch whether the next model holds it. One point is noise, two is a trend change.
items.tweetA: Anthropic's new model just beat the trend line, not just the previous record. The week it files to go public. If AI-assisted R&D is bending the curve, the compute commitments start to look less crazy.
items.tweetB: Epoch now gives probabilities, not just ranks: 72% chance Astra beats Opus 5.5. Model leadership is a distribution, not a podium. Price it that way.

items.title: Global AI compute is doubling every 9 months; Broadcom doubled TPU shipments in one quarter
items.idea: New AI compute capacity is doubling every ~9 months, with quarterly additions growing ~2.5x/yr since 2024, down from ~6x in 2023. Broadcom doubled TPU compute shipments from FQ2 to FQ3 2026 to nearly 2M H100-equivalents: 65% more chips (~800K), plus a mix shift to TPU v7, shipped to Google and Anthropic. TPUs were ~25% of all AI compute shipped worldwide in Apr-Jun.
items.angle: Custom silicon is taking share in compute, not just units. A quarter of global AI compute on TPUs changes the $NVDA vs $AVGO debate.
items.tweetA: Broadcom shipped twice as much TPU compute this quarter as last. TPUs are now ~25% of all AI compute shipped. The 'NVIDIA has 90% share' number is from another era. $AVGO $NVDA $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Compute growth slowed from 6x a year (2023) to 2.5x. Still a doubling every 9 months. Supply roughly 2.5x a year while prices fall. Ask what that does to the value of last year's chips.

items.title: 72% of global AI compute landed in the US since 2022; China 10%, but 18% of chips
items.idea: Epoch's AI Chip Imports explorer: of 27.4M H100-equivalents delivered through June 2026, the US got 72%, China 10%, the EU 5%, Malaysia 2%. China has 18% of chips but 10% of compute, so its chips are weaker; export-compliant and domestic chips are ~40% of its total. Huawei's Horinger (Inner Mongolia) campus: up to 286MW but ~7% of SpaceX's Colossus 2 compute. US facilities get 2.5x more AI compute per unit of power. Horinger should reach ~141K H100e by early 2028; Colossus 2 is expected to pass 1.8M H100e.
items.angle: China's constraint is chips, not energy. Export controls are working on compute density. That raises the stakes on chip diversion stories like the Nvidia/Megaspeed probe.
items.tweetA: China has plenty of power and 18% of the world's AI chips, but only 10% of the compute. Huawei's biggest campus: 286MW for 7% of one Colossus. Export controls aren't stopping chips. They're stopping performance.
items.tweetB: US data centers get 2.5x more AI compute per watt than China's. In a power-constrained buildout, that's the real gap. The Nvidia spy probe matters because the best chips are the only thing China can't build its way to.

items.title: Biologists now cite LLMs almost as often as AlphaFold; math arXiv AI use went from 4% to 48% in 6 months
items.idea: 17% of biology preprints now acknowledge LLM use, nearly matching the 19% acknowledging specialized AI like AlphaFold. LLM use specifically for research or analysis rose from ~1% at the start of 2026 to ~4% in September. In math arXiv preprints, AI-use acknowledgments rose from ~4% in April to 48% by October.
items.angle: Math went from 4% to 48% in six months, an adoption curve. Combined with the Scientific American story on 'dueling proofs', AI-for-science is moving from tools to co-authorship.
items.tweetA: Math papers acknowledging AI use: 4% in April, 48% in October. Half of new math research now involves AI in six months. That's faster than any software adoption curve I've seen.
items.tweetB: Biology is where it matters for money: LLM use for actual research went from 1% to 4% this year. Still small, but compounding. The biotech productivity story starts in the methods section.

items.title: GB300 serves ~25x an H100's agentic inference with only 2.5x the FLOPs; newest chips up to 72x
items.idea: Epoch's new Inference Performance Index (Jason Li) measures how many requests a chip can serve at once across speeds, capturing memory and interconnect. Nvidia's GB300 provides ~25x an H100's inference capacity per chip on agentic workloads, despite only 2.5x the 8-bit FLOP/s. Scored against GB300, newer chips have up to 72x the H100's inference capacity.
items.angle: FLOP/s badly understates inference gains. That makes old-generation GPUs depreciate faster than the 5-6 year accounting lives hyperscalers use, and makes neocloud H100 collateral weaker than it looks.
items.tweetA: GB300: 25x an H100's inference for 2.5x the FLOPs. Newest chips: up to 72x. Now think about neoclouds financing H100s over 6 years. The collateral is aging in dog years. $CRWV
items.tweetB: If inference capacity per chip goes up 25-72x in two generations, 'AI compute scarcity' is temporary by construction. That's the fiber story: capacity per strand up 40x, prices down 70% a year.

items.title: Hugging Face, now owned by Nvidia, hosts 6,500+ 'abliterated' models, some marketed for offensive cyber
items.idea: More than 6,500 models tagged 'abliterated', uncensored or 'heretic' (safety removed) were on Hugging Face in July, and many remain, despite a content policy banning models built for unauthorized access or malicious code. HF took down one GLM-5.3 'abliterated for offensive cyber' model in October, but the same creator (Audnai) still offers others; one claims to refuse only 7.5% of harmful requests. A dealignai GLM-5.3 derivative says it's 'built for offensive cybersecurity' and was tested on keyloggers and ransomware. Anthropic found GLM-5.3 develops browser exploits in 12% of attempts.
items.angle: With Nvidia owning Hugging Face, this becomes $NVDA headline and regulatory risk with Democrats taking power. Together with Epoch's $1K Firefox exploit, it builds the case for regulating open weights.
items.tweetA: Nvidia owns Hugging Face. Hugging Face hosts models that advertise ransomware generation. Epoch just showed one of those base models hacks Firefox for $1,000. That chain will end up in a congressional hearing. $NVDA
items.tweetB: CrowdStrike's CEO: 'frontier capability is available to anyone, regardless of intent, with no guardrails.' He also sells the defense. Cyber budgets go up when the attacker's cost goes to $1K. $CRWD

items.title: Abliteration's inventor is 'torn'; nobody has defined a middle path for open weights
items.idea: Andrew Arditi, whose 2024 paper found the small internal mechanism that controls refusals, says 'we did not expect this to explode' and that there's little thinking on a middle path. Heretic developer Philipp Weidmann says most demand is legitimate (pharma, security research, even Switzerland's Supreme Court translating legal documents) and calls the backlash corporate influence operations (no evidence offered). Thinking Machines has proposed a 'safe path' to open weights.
items.angle: The open-weight policy fight is about to get a forcing event. Expect frontier labs to push for licensing of open weights, and open-weight advocates to point to over-refusal. Watch Thinking Machines' proposal as a possible compromise template.
items.tweetA: Switzerland's Supreme Court reportedly tried an uncensored model because mainstream AI refused to translate legal documents. Over-cautious guardrails are pushing legitimate users toward models with no guardrails at all.
items.tweetB: A refusal can be removed by deleting one small part of the model. That means 'safe open weights' isn't a technical problem today. It's distribution policy. Regulation will target hosting platforms, not models.

items.source: This Week in AI / TWiAI Demo
items.title: One Notion 'brain' shared by Claude, Codex and Grok Bot: first audit scored 57/100, 88 after fixes
items.idea: Notion released a shared memory for AI agents via its MCP server. TWiAI connected Claude, Codex and Grok Bot to it for a week. Grok read the show's rules unprompted; Claude stopped instead of guessing when it couldn't reach brand files. A twice-weekly Claude routine audited the brain: 57/100 on the first run, 88 after fixes. MCP reads/writes don't use Notion AI credits, and agents can see the whole workspace, not just the brain pages.
items.angle: Cross-vendor agent memory moves lock-in from the model to the context store. Whoever owns persistent memory (Notion, Supermemory, Zep) owns switching costs. Privacy scope ('sees your whole workspace') is the catch.
items.tweetA: Three agents from three rival companies, one shared memory in Notion. The model is the commodity now. The lock-in is wherever your context lives.
items.tweetB: Notion's agent memory doesn't charge AI credits for MCP reads and writes. It's giving away the memory layer to become the system of record for every agent. Same playbook as owning the database.
